extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and researchers in linguistics, pragmatics, and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for analyzing, classifying, and researching verbal and non-verbal humor from a linguistic/pragmatic perspective, including theoretical models (script theory, IDM, spreading activation), empirical methods, and scholarly practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological goal: necessary and sufficient conditions for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The research aim (following Raskin 1985) is to determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for humor to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the central methodological objective as explicating the conditions under which humor arises; use explicit theorizing and comparison of competing accounts. This is presented as a guiding aim for rigorous theory-building in the linguistics of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isotopy-Disjunction Model (IDM): three narrative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide jokes into three narrative functions: (1) introduction of situation and characters, (2) creation of expectation (often containing an ambiguous 'connector'), and (3) the final part responsible for the humor, containing a word/phrase that reveals the hidden isotopy (the 'disjunctor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply IDM when analyzing joke texts: identify connector and disjunctor, note that the third function typically appears at the end of the joke. Attardo combines IDM with verbal/referential distinctions and uses quantitative evidence to support differing structures across joke types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal vs. referential joke distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and classify jokes as verbal or referential: these categories have different structural profiles and distribution (Attardo's corpus shows a speakers' preference for referential jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or modeling jokes, distinguish which category a joke belongs to, since different explanatory mechanisms and structures apply; use corpus evidence to confirm category-specific patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns analysis: phonemic distance, metalinguistic nature, Cratylism, and spreading activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze puns beyond taxonomy by examining phonemic distance (paronomasia), treating puns as metalinguistic phenomena, considering a Cratylistic view that sounds can be more motivated, and invoking spreading activation in speech production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ phonemic-distance metrics (e.g., Sobkowiak-style analyses) and cognitive mechanisms (spreading activation) to explain when homonyms/paronyms are treated as synonymous in playful contexts. Avoid limiting study to typologies; instead link phonological, semantic, and production processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiotic / bisociation approaches: global viewpoint including visual humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt semiotic (bisociation) theories for a global, semantic-oriented perspective that can incorporate non-verbal and visual humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semiotic/bisociation perspectives when addressing multimodal or visual humor; recognize these approaches are less formalized than strictly linguistic models but offer valuable global insights and pointers for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script theory and General Theory of Verbal Humor: multi-parameter similarity model
rubrics_metrics.description: Use script theory as a formal semantic framework for humor and the General Theory of Verbal Humor which examines joke similarity via multiple parameters: logical mechanisms, situation, target, narrative strategy, and language (in addition to script opposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling joke similarity or representation, evaluate across these five parameters rather than relying solely on script opposition; distinguish applications that use script theory in standard form from those that require theoretical revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register-based humor: prototype/polythetic definition and register criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Define registers not by single necessary features but via a prototype/polythetic approach (criteria such as subject matter, linguistic features, social roles/fields), and define register-based humor as the overlapping (concomitant) activation of two or more scripts among which at least two are in a relationship of (local) antonymy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prototype/polythetic categorization instead of strict boundaries; require weak activation so the serious message can persist. Apply script-theory and spreading-activation together to analyze register-clash humor (example: DOG vs. CHILD scripts in 'doggie').

rubrics_metrics.name: Spreading-activation model for multilayered and association-driven humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the spreading-activation model to analyze multilayered literary texts and association-driven humor (texts with little internal consistency rely on associations rather than a single script opposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer spreading-activation for complex, multilayered, or associative humor (e.g., certain literary passages, menu-propos) where script theory is less adequate; the model can handle multiple simultaneous activations and weak associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative nature of humor: maxims, hierarchy, and BF/NBF continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat humor as cooperative behavior that violates conversational maxims at an initial stage but remains cooperative; recognize a hierarchy/weights among maxims (quantity and relevance more significant), reject simplistic maxim-flouting or 'mere mention' accounts, and place bona-fide (BF) and non-bona-fide (NBF) modes on a negotiable continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model humor as negotiated BF/NBF blending where presuppositional bases convey factual information (secondary social function). Use conversation analysis to test claims and consider revising concepts like Raskin's BF mode to accommodate maxim hierarchy and negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/corpus methods: quantitative confirmation of structures and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantitative corpus research to confirm structural distinctions (e.g., between joke categories) and speakers' preferences (e.g., prevalence of referential jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support theoretical claims with corpus counts and quantitative analyses; Attardo's own corpus work is cited as confirming category-specific structures and distributional tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly practice: comprehensive literature survey and accurate bibliographic/indexing apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain comprehensive, accurately referenced bibliographies and complete indexes; conduct representative surveys to avoid duplication of prior results and redundant research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough, correctly indexed bibliography prevents repetition and helps cumulative progress. The reviewer criticizes missing/incorrect parenthetical references and incomplete name-indexing as impediments—so ensure bibliographic completeness and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/textbook design: clear structure with numbered sections and summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize textbook material into short, clearly numbered sections and subsections with mid- and end-chapter summaries and evaluations to aid clarity and teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic chapter layout to make a textbook-style synthesis accessible. Note that such meticulous division may cause some repetition or over-signposting, but overall aids learners and classroom use.
